questions.question: A surgical procedure is performed on the great saphenous vein, around 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus. Which of the following structures is most likely to be injured?

explanation.text: The great saphenous vein passes anterior to the medial malleolus and is closely associated with the saphenous nerve; therefore, it is more prone to injury during this procedure. Great Saphenous Vein Origin: Begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch. Course: Ascends 2.5 cm in front of the medial malleolus, along the medial aspect of the tibia with the saphenous nerve. Passes posterior to the medial condyles of the tibia and femur.

Runs posterior to the patella and ascends along the medial side of the femur. Pierces the cribriform fascia and passes through the saphenous opening. Drains into the femoral vein after piercing the femoral sheath. Clinical

Aspects Venesection: Performed at the ankle in emergencies. Care must be taken to avoid damaging the saphenous nerve (as it accompanies the vein). Coronary Bypass Surgery: Commonly used as a graft for bypass surgery. The vein must be reversed to prevent its valves from obstructing blood flow in the graft.

questions.question: A 34-year-old female, who works as a maid complained of knee pain and swelling. Which of the following area gets damaged in Housemaid’s knee?

explanation.text: B (Prepatellar bursa) The correct answer is option b (Prepatellar bursa), as housemaid's knee involves inflammation of the prepatellar bursa due to repeated kneeling or trauma to the front of the knee.Housemaid's knee, also known as prepatellar bursitis, involves inflammation of the prepatellar bursa. The prepatellar bursa is located just in front of the patella (kneecap) and can become inflamed due to repetitive kneeling or trauma to the area.

This condition is often seen in individuals who perform activities that involve prolonged kneeling, such as housemaids or carpet layers. Incorrect Options: Option A - A (Suprapatellar bursa): The suprapatellar bursa is located above the patella (kneecap) and helps reduce friction between the femur (thigh bone) and the quadriceps tendon. This bursa is not commonly associated with housemaid's knee.

Option C - C (Infrapatellar bursa): The infrapatellar bursa is located below the patella, between the patellar ligament and the tibia (shin bone). It helps reduce friction during knee movements. Inflammation of this bursa is known as "clergyman's knee" or "Clergyman's bursitis," which is caused by excessive kneeling and friction.

Option D - D (Pes anserine bursa): The pes anserine bursa is located on the inner side of the knee, just below the joint. It is situated between the tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles and the underlying tibia. Inflammation of this bursa can lead to pes anserine bursitis, which typically presents as pain and tenderness on the inner side of the knee. This condition is not directly related to housemaid's knee.

This nerve provides motor innervation to the gluteus maximus, which is the largest muscle in the buttocks and plays a significant role in movements such as hip extension and external rotation.

questions.question: Which of the following arteries is palpated in the image shown below?

explanation.text: The artery palpated in the image shown is the posterior tibial artery; it is palpated between the medial malleolus and Achilles tendon/tendocalcaneous. Locate the medial malleolus (the bony bump on the inside of the ankle). Place your index and middle fingers on the inside of the ankle and move your fingers behind the medial malleolus towards the back of the leg. You should be able to feel the posterior tibial artery pulsations in this area.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Anterior tibial artery: To palpate the anterior tibial artery, ask the patient to lie down or sit with their legs slightly bent. Locate the ankle bones (medial malleolus and lateral malleolus) and identify the space between them. Place your index and middle fingers on the space between the ankle bones and move your fingers upwards towards the top of the foot.

You should be able to feel the anterior tibial artery pulsations in this area. Option C - Dorsalis pedis artery: To palpate the dorsalis pedis artery, ask the patient to lie down or sit with their legs slightly bent. Locate the first and second metatarsal bones (the bones that

connect to the big toe). Place your index and middle fingers on the top of the foot, just below the space between the first and second metatarsal bones, you can feel the pulsations there. Option D - Popliteal artery: To palpate the popliteal artery, ask the patient to lie down on their stomach or to sit with their legs hanging off the edge of the exam table. Flex the knee to about 90 degrees.

Use your fingers to locate the popliteal fossa, which is the small depression behind the knee joint. Feel for the pulsation of the artery in the middle of the fossa. Press your fingers gently into the popliteal fossa and feel for the pulsation of the artery.

questions.question: What is the ligament that links the medial cuneiform bone to the base of the second metatarsal bone?

explanation.text: The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal. It is a strong oblique ligament that stabilises the tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint and prevents excessive movement between

the midfoot and forefoot. Injury to this ligament leads to a Lisfranc injury, which involves displacement of the second metatarsal and can result in significant midfoot instability. Anatomy: The Lisfranc joint is formed by the metatarsal bones (M1 to M5) and the tarsal bones (cuneiform C1 to C3 and cuboid). The Lisfranc ligament is a 3 part structure that joins the medial cuneiform to the 2nd metatarsal.

Interdigitating joints and strong ligaments support the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The second metatarsal base fits into a recess formed by the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms. Injury Mechanism: Dislocations are rare and typically arise from twisting or crushing injuries, with the foot buckling at the midfoot–forefoot junction. Often considered high-energy injuries, leading to extensive damage to the foot.

The direction of forefoot dislocation is not useful for treatment guidance or outcome prediction. Clinical Features: Suspect TMT dislocation or fracture-dislocation in patients with foot pain and swelling after high-velocity impacts (e.g., car accidents, falls). About 20–30% of these injuries are initially missed. Obvious deformity usually only occurs with severe injuries.

Imaging: X-rays: Interpretation can be challenging; systematic examination is crucial. Focus on the alignment of the second and fourth metatarsals (oblique view): The medial edge of the second metatarsal should align with the medial edge of the second cuneiform. The medial edge of the fourth metatarsal should align with the medial side of the cuboid. A true lateral view may show dorsal displacement of the second metatarsal base.

Advanced Imaging: If fracture-dislocation is suspected, stress views may help, but a CT scan is more effective for assessing the extent of injury. Treatment: Undisplaced Sprains: Require 4–6 weeks of cast or boot immobilization. Subluxation or Dislocation: Accurate reduction is necessary, often achieved through traction and manipulation under anesthesia.

The position is stabilized with percutaneous K-wires or screws, followed by cast immobilization (non-weight-bearing for 6–8 weeks). Open Reduction: If closed reduction fails, open reduction is essential. Exposure of the second metatarsal base via a longitudinal incision for joint manipulation. Fixation with K-wires or screws, followed by immobilization.

Complications: Compartment Syndrome: A tense, swollen foot may indicate serious compartment syndrome. Measure intracompartmental pressures if suspected. Prompt decompression through surgical incisions is critical; the wound is left open until swelling subsides.

Chopart ligament (option A): Related to the Chopart joint, which is the midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint, connecting the hindfoot (talus and calcaneus) to the midfoot (navicular and cuboid). Not involved in the medial cuneiform–second metatarsal connection. Spring ligament (option B): Also called the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, it connects the calcaneus to the navicular and supports the medial longitudinal arch of the foot.

Does not link the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal. Deltoid ligament (option D): A strong medial ankle ligament, stabilising the talus within the ankle mortise. It is unrelated to the tarsometatarsal joints.

questions.question: Identify the tarsal bone labeled in the image below.

explanation.text: The navicular bone is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located on the medial side of the foot, between the talus (posteriorly) and the cuneiform bones (anteriorly). The X-ray shows a lateral view of the foot, with the navicular bone labeled in its characteristic position between the talus and the midfoot structures. Tarsal Bones and Their Positions Bone Group Bones Description & Function Tarsals Provide mechanical support and structure to the foot.

Proximal Group Talus Transmits body weight to the foot. Articulates at three joints: Superiorly: Ankle joint (tibia/fibula) Inferiorly: Subtalar joint (calcaneus) Anteriorly: Talonavicular joint (navicular) Calcaneus Largest tarsal bone, forms the heel. Articulates at two joints: Superiorly: Subtalar joint (talus) Anteriorly: Calcaneocuboid joint (cuboid) Intermediate Group Navicular Boat-shaped; articulates with talus, cuneiforms, and cuboid.

Has a tuberosity for tibialis posterior tendon attachment. Distal Group Cuboid Lateral; articulates with calcaneus and fourth/fifth metatarsals. Features a groove for fibularis longus tendon. Cuneiforms (3) Medial, intermediate, lateral; wedge-shaped. Help form the transverse arch; attach to various muscles. Metatarsals I-V (1-5) Connect tarsals to phalanges; numbered medial to lateral.

Have a head, neck, shaft, and base; facilitate movement and support. Phalanges Great Toe: 2 (proximal, distal) Toes 2-5: 3 each (proximal, intermediate, distal). Each phalanx has a base, shaft, and head; provide structure to toes.
**Calcaneus (Option A):** Incorrect because the calcaneus is located posteriorly and is the largest tarsal bone forming the heel.
**Cuboid (Option B):** Incorrect because the cuboid is on the lateral side of the foot, articulating with the 4th and 5th metatarsals.
**Talus (Option D):** Incorrect because the talus is superior to the navicular, articulating with the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint.

questions.question: The prevention of lateral dislocation of the patella during knee flexion is by-

explanation.text: The vastus medialis, particularly its oblique fibers (VMO - Vastus Medialis Obliquus), plays a crucial role in preventing lateral dislocation of the patella by exerting a medial pull on the patella during knee flexion. This counteracts the lateral pull of the quadriceps, especially the vastus lateralis.

Patellar Stability and Dislocation Prevention Structure Role in Patellar Stability Vastus Medialis (VMO) Exerts a medial pull on the patella, preventing lateral displacement Patellar Ligament Connects the patella to the tibial tuberosity but does not prevent lateral dislocation Gracilis A medial thigh muscle responsible for hip adduction, not involved in patellar stability Rectus Femoris A major knee extensor, but does not prevent lateral displacement Patellar Ligament (Option B): Incorrect because it primarily stabilizes the patella in the superior-inferior direction, not against lateral forces.
**Gracilis (Option C):** Incorrect because it is a medial thigh muscle involved in hip adduction and does not influence patellar stability.
**Rectus Femoris (Option D):** Incorrect because it is a knee extensor, contributing to overall quadriceps function but not directly preventing lateral patellar displacement.

questions.question: Which of the following branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? 1. Superior gluteal artery 2. Inferior gluteal artery 3. Superior vesical artery 4. Middle rectal artery 5. Inferior vesical artery 6. Vaginal artery

explanation.text: The anterior division of the internal iliac artery gives rise to multiple visceral and parietal branches supplying the pelvic organs, perineum, and lower limb. The correct answer includes all the relevant branches from this division.

Branches of the Internal Iliac Artery: Division Branches Anterior Division (Primarily supplies pelvic organs, perineum, and medial thigh) Inferior gluteal artery, superior vesical artery, middle rectal artery, inferior vesical artery, vaginal artery, obturator artery, internal pudendal artery, uterine artery Posterior Division (Primarily supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region) Superior gluteal artery, iliolumbar artery, lateral sacral artery 1,2,3,5- (Option A): Incorrect because superior gluteal artery (1) belongs to the posterior division. 2,3,4,6- (Option B): Incorrect because it excludes inferior vesical artery (5), which is an anterior division branch. 1,4,5,6- (Option D): Incorrect because superior gluteal artery (1) belongs to the posterior division.

questions.question: A boy with a history of a fall from a tree presents with a lurching gait and dragging of his feet. Which of the following structures are involved?

explanation.text: The gluteus medius is essential for stabilizing the pelvis during walking. Injury to this muscle or its innervation (superior gluteal nerve) leads to a lurching gait (Trendelenburg gait) where the patient compensates by shifting weight toward the affected side to prevent pelvic drop.

Gluteus Muscles and Trendelenburg Gait Tensor Fasciae Latae Gluteus Medius Gluteus Minimus Attachments Origin: Outer lip of the iliac crest extending from the anterior superior iliac spine to the tubercle of the crest. Insertion: Iliotibial tract 3–5 cm below the level of the greater trochanter.

Origin: Gluteal surface of the ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines Insertion: Oblique ridge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. Origin: Gluteal surfaces of the ilium between anterior & inferior gluteal lines.

Insertion: Anterior aspect of the Greater trochanter Relations Between gluteus medius and sartorius Covered by fascia lata Covered by gluteus maximus (posterior third) Deep to gluteus minimus Deep to gluteus medius Related to hip joint capsule Vascular Supply Mainly from lateral circumflex femoral artery Supplied by superior gluteal artery Deep branch of superior gluteal artery Trochanteric anastomosis Main trunk and deep branch of superior gluteal arter y Trochanteric anastomosis Innervation Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Actions Hip flexor and abductor Stabilizes pelvis Helps maintain extended knee Abducts thigh Medial & lateral rotation of thigh Supports pelvis during single-leg stance Abducts thigh Medial and lateral rotation of thigh Testing Depression below anterior superior iliac spine Abduction against resistance Medial rotation against resistance Abduction against resistance Medial rotation against resistance Abduction against resistance Trendelenberg sign: When the body's weight is balanced on one leg, the gluteal muscles on the supported side help elevate the opposite, unsupported side of the pelvis.

However, if there is a malfunction in the abductor mechanism, the Sound side sinks, which is referred to as a positive Trendelenburg sign (uncompensated). This sign indicates issues with hip abductors, such as paralysis of the gluteus medius and minimus; problems with the fulcrum, including congenital or pathological hip dislocations; and concerns related to body weight, such as an unhealed fracture of the femoral neck.

When patients with the gluteus medius and minimus paralysis walk, they have a characteristic lurching gait i.e., during the single leg supporting phase of walking, there is leaning of the trunk to the affected side known as the compensated Trendelenburg sign. Duck waddling gait is seen when both the sides are affected. 1 (Gluteus maximus) (Option

A): Incorrect – Gluteus maximus is responsible for hip extension. Injury causes difficulty in rising from a seated position but does not cause a lurching gait. 3 (Piriformis) (Option C): Incorrect – Piriformis primarily functions in hip external rotation.

Injury leads to piriformis syndrome, which causes sciatica-like pain but does not cause a lurching gait. 4 (Sciatic nerve) (Option D): Incorrect – Sciatic nerve injury causes foot drop and weakness in knee flexion rather than a Trendelenburg gait.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the embryonic development of the heart is incorrect?

options.A: Heart tube is derived from the splanchnopleuric mesoderm.
options.B: Truncus arteriosus forms the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
options.C: Bulbus cordis is located at the caudal end of the developing heart tube.
options.D: Disappearance of the dorsal mesocardium creates the transverse sinus.

explanation.text: Bulbus cordis is located at the cranial end of the developing heart tube, not the caudal end. Formation of Heart Tubes: The endothelial heart tube is derived from the splanchnopleuric mesoderm, located near the pericardial cavity. (Option A) Initially, the heart appears as right and left endothelial heart tubes. These tubes fuse to form a single heart tube.

The heart tube has 5 dilatations, which are: Truncus arteriosus Bulbus cordis Primitive ventricle Primitive atrium Sinus venosus Sinus venosus is located at the caudal (venous) end of the primitive heart tube. It consists of a body with two prolongations known as the right and left horns. Right horn: Forms smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). Left horn: Forms coronary sinus.

Each horn receives blood from three veins: Vitelline vein Umbilical vein Common cardinal vein Bulbus cordis is the cranial most part of the developing heart tube. (Option C) Forms outflow (smooth) parts of the right ventricle (conus arteriosus) and left ventricle (aortic vestibule). Primitive ventricle: Forms inflow (rough) parts of both ventricles. Primitive atrium: Forms trabeculated part of the right and left atrium.

Truncus arteriosus: Forms ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. (Option B) Formation of Transverse Pericardial Sinus: Heart Tube Folding: Brings the arterial and venous ends closer together. Disappearance of the dorsal mesocardium creates the transverse sinus of the pericardium. (Option D) Parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium become continuous at the arterial and venous ends of the heart.
Pericardium forms two tubes: One enclosing the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Other enclosing the SVC, IVC, and four pulmonary veins. Two tubes are separated by the transverse sinus of the pericardium.

questions.question: A newborn baby is found to have bluish discoloration of lips, tongue, and nails with poor feeding and signs of congestive heart failure. She is diagnosed with patent truncus arteriosus. What developmental error leads to this condition?

options.B: Switching of the aorta and pulmonary artery position.
options.D: Complete absence of the spiral septum

explanation.text: The absence of spiral aorticopulmonary septum (AP septum) is a pathologic finding in truncus arteriosus (TA). Formation of the Bulbus Cordis: The bulbus cordis is the cranial-most region of the primitive heart tube, Originates from the cardiogenic area, a specialized mesoderm region cranial to the prochordal plate. Divides into 3 parts: Proximal one-third: Merges with the primitive ventricle to form the bulboventricular chamber.

Contributes to the trabeculated part of the right ventricle. Middle part (Conus Cordis): Forms outflow tracts of both ventricles. Two septae are formed in this: proximal and distal bulbar septa. The proximal septum contributes to the interventricular septum. The distal septum divides the conus into the aortic vestibule and conus arteriosus.

Distal part (Truncus Arteriosus): Divides into ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk via the spiral aortopulmonary septum Spiral septum is formed by the fusion of the right superior and left inferior truncus swellings or cushions. Responsible for distributing blood to the body and lungs.

Clinical Significance: Persistent truncus arteriosus: Complete absence of spiral septum. (Option D) Ventricular Septal Defects (VSDs): Result from incomplete closure of the interventricular septum, leading to holes in the ventricular wall. (Option C) Symptoms may include shortness of breath and an increased risk of infections.

Tetralogy of Fallot: Comprises four defects linked to abnormalities in the conus and truncus arteriosus: VSD Overriding aorta Pulmonary stenosis (Option A) Right ventricular hypertrophy Can cause cyanosis and impede blood flow to the lungs.

Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA): Occurs when the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched due to errors in truncus arteriosus division. (Option B) Requires surgical intervention to correct blood flow issues.

questions.question: An infant's echocardiogram reveals an enlarged coronary sinus. This finding most likely results from an abnormality in which embryological structure?

options.A: Right horn of the sinus venosus
options.B: Left horn of the sinus venosus

explanation.text: Left horn of the sinus venosus regresses during development to form the coronary sinus, so a defect in this structure can result in an abnormal coronary sinus. Sinus Venosus: Structure of Sinus Venosus Sinus venosus is the caudal (venous) end of the primitive heart tube, consisting of a body with right and left horns.

Each horn is connected to three major veins: Vitelline vein (from the yolk sac) Umbilical vein (from the placenta) Common cardinal vein (from the body wall) Communication with Atrial Chamber Sinus venosus initially communicates with the primitive atrium through a wide sinoatrial orifice. Grooves appear on the lateral walls of the heart, partially separating the sinus venosus from the atrium.
Regression of the Left Horn Left horn and its tributaries become reduced in size and become part of the coronary sinus.

**Fate of Right Horn (Option A):** Incorporated into the right atrium, forming the smooth-walled part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). Fate of Sinus Venosus Tributaries Right common cardinal vein becomes part of the superior vena cava. (Option C) Right vitelline vein forms the terminal part of the inferior vena cava. (Option D) Left horn regresses and becomes part of the coronary sinus. (Option B) Left common cardinal vein forms the oblique vein of the left atrium.
